html:
The killing of Hipparchus, brother of the tyrant Hippias of Athens, by two Athenian lovers, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, during the Panathenaic festival of 514 BCE.

Thucydides says the motive was personal: Hipparchus had pursued Harmodius and, when rejected, insulted his sister. The two meant to kill Hippias too but failed. Harmodius was cut down on the spot, and Aristogeiton was caught and killed. Hippias, the son of Pisistratus, then ruled more harshly until 510 BCE, when a Spartan army under King Cleomenes drove him out.

The democracy that Cleisthenes founded soon after honoured the pair as the tyrant slayers who freed Athens. A bronze statue group of them stood in the Agora; when Xerxes carried it off in 480 BCE, Athens put up a new one. Thucydides wrote partly to correct this popular legend.
sum: The killing of Hipparchus, brother of the tyrant Hippias of Athens, by two Athenian lovers, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, during the Panathenaic festival of 514 BCE.
